L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Flat 12% personal income tax (KPMG; Deloitte 2026). Residents are domiciled in Moldova or present at least 183 days in the tax year. On scope, PwC (2026) and Deloitte 2026 both say residents are taxed on income related to activities performed in Moldova (PwC adds Moldovan-source income), while the older KPMG guide (2023) says worldwide. PRACTICAL ANSWER: either way, a freelancer living and working in Moldova is taxed there on income from foreign clients. For the IT Park single tax (companies), see L7.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: Standard VAT is 20%, with reduced 8% and 0% bands. From March 2026, a resident business must register for VAT once turnover in the last 12 consecutive months reaches MDL 1.7 million. The threshold was raised from MDL 1.2 million, via an interim MDL 1.5 million from 1 January 2026, to MDL 1.7 million on 1 March 2026. Voluntary registration is possible. Foreign B2C digital services are taxed at 20%, with simplified registration for non-residents.

sources.title: Moldova - Corporate - Other taxes
sources.quote: Starting March 2026, a company is required to register for VAT purposes if the total turnover within the last 12 consecutive months reached the threshold of MDL 1.7 million.

sources.title: Moldova - Corporate - Other taxes

L7_incentives.question: Legal incentives / tax holidays / special zones relevant to small digital businesses
L7_incentives.answer: Moldova IT Park (Law 77/2016): a resident IT company pays a single 7% tax on turnover in place of six separate taxes, state-guaranteed to 2035. Residency depends on the 70% rule (share of revenue from qualifying IT activities). It is a company regime, so an individual freelancer would need a company to use it.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: Stripe does not accept merchants here; Wise does not let residents hold money. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Send, receive, and withdraw'). (6) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
